title: Waddling Through the Shallows: Divers Discover a New Walking Shark in Papua New Guinea
summary: What has fins, spots, and literally walks on the ocean floor? A newly discovered shark that's rewriting what we know about marine life. Divers off the coast of Papua New Guinea have identified a fresh species of walking shark, a rare type of carpet shark that uses its pectoral and pelvic fins to amble across shallow reefs. Named Hemiscyllium dudgeonae—or Dudgeon's walking shark—this small, brown-spotted creature was found in dark waters barely a meter deep. The discovery was a serendipitous twist. Christine Dudgeon, a senior research fellow at the University of the Sunshine Coast, was actually searching for another walking shark, Michael's walking shark, which sports leopard-like prints. When her team hauled up an unfamiliar specimen, doctoral student Jess Blakeway immediately noticed the difference. "Chris, it's different," she called out. The new shark's body was covered in small white dashes and brown dots—a pattern distinct from any known species. Within two days, the researchers located 11 more individuals across three sites, including juveniles and adults, all bearing the same markings. Genetic analysis back in Australia confirmed their hunch: this was an undescribed species. The finding, published in the Journal of the Ocean Science Foundation, brings the total number of walking shark species to 10. What makes these sharks so unusual? Unlike their open-ocean cousins, walking sharks spend their entire lives on coral reefs. Their ability to "walk" is a crucial adaptation for low tide, when parts of the reef become isolated and oxygen levels plummet. By wriggling across the seafloor, they can continue hunting small prey even in hypoxic conditions—a skill that may have evolved to cope with the dramatic shifts of tropical reef flats. Some species can survive in low-oxygen environments for hours, though scientists are still unraveling the exact mechanisms. So far, Dudgeon's walking shark has been documented at only three locations in Papua New Guinea. If its range is truly that restricted, it could be vulnerable to habitat degradation, climate change, or overfishing. Many walking sharks exhibit strong site fidelity, meaning they rarely stray from their birthplace, which limits their ability to recolonize damaged areas. This discovery underscores how much biodiversity remains hidden in shallow waters, often overlooked in favor of deep-sea exploration. "Finding something in very shallow water is unusual and highlights that there is potentially a lot of biodiversity that we really don't know about," Dudgeon said. Her team plans to continue surveys in the region, hoping to learn more about this enigmatic new resident of the reef.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that unknown species are not just hiding in deep ocean chasms but also in knee-deep water where kids swim; understanding these creatures could help protect entire reef ecosystems that billions of people rely on for food and coastal protection.

background_read: Walking sharks belong to the carpet shark family, which also includes wobbegongs and the giant whale shark; most live in the warm waters of the western Pacific.

Papua New Guinea (an island nation just north of Australia) sits inside the Coral Triangle, a region with more marine species than anywhere else on Earth, but much of its shallow reef life remains unstudied.

Christine Dudgeon (a marine biologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia) has been studying these unusual sharks for years; they are known for their spots and ability to survive in extremely low oxygen.
Earlier walking shark discoveries include Michael's walking shark (named after a photographer) and the epaulette shark, which can slow its heartbeat to cope with oxygen-poor tide pools.
Scientists often publish new species in journals like the Journal of the Ocean Science Foundation to officially record and describe them so other researchers can verify and study the creatures.

perspectives.description: Biologists celebrate each new walking shark because it adds a piece to the puzzle of how marine life adapts to extreme conditions. Every species also helps make the case for stronger conservation of coral reefs, which are under threat from warming seas.

If Dudgeon's walking shark truly lives in only a handful of tiny areas, a single pollution event, storm, or bout of overfishing could wipe the entire species out. Many walking sharks cannot easily move to new reefs, making local protection urgent.

The ability to 'walk' and tolerate low oxygen isn't just a party trick—it's a window into how some sharks might survive a changing climate. Scientists study these traits to understand resilience in reef fish over millions of years.

Local governments in Papua New Guinea and international researchers now face a decision: act quickly to safeguard the known sites, or risk losing a species before it's even fully understood. Future surveys may reveal more hidden hotspots, but they also need funding and community involvement.
